project: The Stock Market: From the Ground Up

items.whyBetter: CME describes risk-based size from planned stop distance and account risk; 160 shares is an independent whole-share fictional case.
items.limitations: CME examples cover contracts and stop references; stock whole-share size, gaps, fees and broker rules require separate validation.

items.whyBetter: Risk per position is stop distance × size; open portfolio heat is the sum of non-negative planned stop losses divided by equity.
items.limitations: Portfolio-heat label is an educational convention; specify initial versus current stop and do not treat stop-based risk as maximum actual loss. Secondary source is practitioner context, not an independent professional certification.

items.whyBetter: The Van Tharp Institute explicitly defines R-multiple as realized gain/loss divided by initial planned risk; original 225/150=1.5R arithmetic.
items.limitations: Record gross-versus-net gain convention and treatment of fees. Van Tharp teaching content is reference-only, not licensed for republishing.

items.whyBetter: SEC explains borrowed shares and financing costs; Nasdaq describes stock lending fees and borrow availability.
items.limitations: The 18% rate, $5,000 basis and 3/360 convention are fictional; lender fee, rebate, marking and day-count conventions depend on broker agreements.

items.whyBetter: FINRA distinguishes reported short positions from daily short-sale volume; short interest/dated float alone does not establish future covering demand.
items.limitations: Short interest and float estimates have differing timestamps and definitions; a 20% ratio is not a predictable squeeze signal.

items.whyBetter: CME trade-plan self-evaluation explicitly includes a daily total-dollar loss limit; fictional realized loss plus fees reaches the declared threshold.
items.limitations: A personal educational loss-state rule is not a broker-enforced shutoff, margin rule or exchange circuit breaker; account P&L inclusion rules must be defined.

items.whyBetter: Risk-of-ruin models require explicit thresholds, risk size, payoff distribution, horizon and dependence assumptions; original +1R/-1R examples measure expectancy only.
items.limitations: The 55% and 48% cases calculate expected R, not a numerical risk-of-ruin probability. Vendor research is illustrative; no calibrated risk-of-ruin conclusion is supported.

items.whyBetter: CFA Institute distinguishes time-weighted from money-weighted returns when external cash flows affect a portfolio; the fictional immediate-deposit shortcut is defined explicitly.
items.limitations: A 5% simple return with an immediate contribution is a narrow scenario; midperiod external flows require dated cash-flow methods, often linked TWR or MWR/IRR.

items.whyBetter: CFA Institute notes that daily volatility × sqrt(number of business days) assumes uncorrelated daily returns; 1.2%×sqrt(252)≈19.0% is a conditional illustration.
items.limitations: Serial correlation, volatility clustering, calendar conventions, sample degrees of freedom and nonstationarity can invalidate a naive scaling.

items.whyBetter: QuantConnect's explicit survivorship-bias section describes the danger of excluding delisted historical constituents; fictional 2/10 omission=20%.
items.limitations: Research guide and source documentation support the issue, but do not certify that any specific uploaded dataset is survivorship-bias free.

items.whyBetter: SEC-hosted issuer materials provide concrete rights-offering ratios and dilution disclosures; fictional 1-for-4 on 10m shares adds 2.5m if fully exercised.
items.limitations: Issuer filings are context-specific and not SEC endorsements. Rights ratios, subscription price, full subscription, percentage ownership and economic dilution must be distinguished; do not copy prospectus text.

notes: SEC investor bulletins, FINRA public education, CFA Institute, CME, QuantConnect and private educational explanations were researched as source pointers only.
No third-party article/chart/code/media/data republication or license grant is assumed.
Owner draft-authoring snapshot remains accepted as historical milestone; two revised source batches require new independent source/content review.
The risk-of-ruin example is expectancy arithmetic, NOT a calculated probability of ruin.
